title: Review: Kinetic and potential energy; conservation; Work–energy theorem and dissipative forces; Power and efficiency; Charge and current
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: E03-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; EL01-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; E02-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; E02-1#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: E02-1#N.4a, E03-1#N.15, E04-1#N.11, EL01-1#N.3, E02-1#N.12, E03-1#N.4a, E04-1#N.3, EL01-1#N.12, EL01-1#N.6a. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Power
items.clue: Rate of doing work, or rate of energy transfer.

items.label: Current
items.clue: Rate of flow of charge through a cross-section.

items.label: Mechanical energy
items.clue: Sum that stays constant when there is no friction or drag.

items.label: Gravitational potential energy
items.clue: Store that depends on position, lost as a dropped ball speeds up.

questions.stem: Object A has mass m and moves at speed 2v. Object B has mass 2m and moves at speed v. What is the kinetic energy of object A divided by the kinetic energy of object B?

options.text: ½

questions.explanation: A: ½m(2v)² = 2mv². B: ½(2m)v² = mv². So A has twice B's kinetic energy: doubling the speed multiplies it by 4, doubling the mass only by 2.

questions.stem: Motor A raises a 200 N load through 3.0 m in 6.0 s. Motor B raises a 100 N load through 6.0 m in 4.0 s. Both lift at constant speed. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A develops more power, as it lifts the heavier load.
B does more work, as it lifts its load twice as high.
Both do equal work, and B develops more power.
Both develop equal power, as they do equal work.

questions.explanation: Each does 600 J (200 × 3.0 and 100 × 6.0). B does it in less time: 600 ÷ 4.0 = 150 W against 600 ÷ 6.0 = 100 W.

questions.stem: A block on a level, frictionless surface is sped up by a constant horizontal force. The work needed to speed the block up from rest to speed v is W. How many times W is needed to speed the block up from v to 3v?

In an electron beam in a vacuum tube, 1.5 × 10¹⁵ electrons pass through a cross-section of the beam in 8.0 s at a steady rate. What is the magnitude of the current in the beam? Use e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

Three identical stones are thrown from the top of a sea cliff with the same speed: one straight up, one horizontally and one straight down. Air resistance is negligible. Which stone hits the sea with the greatest speed?

options.text: The one thrown straight down, as its velocity starts in the direction of gravity.
The one thrown upwards, as it falls back from a greater height than the others.
The one thrown horizontally, as it keeps its horizontal speed while gaining vertical speed.
All land at equal speeds: same starting kinetic energy, same drop in height.

questions.explanation: Initial kinetic energy + potential energy lost = final kinetic energy, and both terms are equal for all three stones. The speeds are equal; only the directions and times of flight differ.

questions.stem: A cyclist rides along a level road at a constant speed of 8.0 m s⁻¹. The total resistive force on the cyclist and bicycle is 25 N. What power does the cyclist's driving force develop?

options.text: 0 W

questions.explanation: At constant speed the driving force equals the resistive force, 25 N. P = Fv = 25 × 8.0 = 200 W.

questions.stem: A child on a toboggan slides across level snow. The child and toboggan have a total mass of 50 kg and slow down from 8.0 m s⁻¹ to 6.0 m s⁻¹. What is the magnitude of the net work done on the child–toboggan system during this time?
A copper wire has a thick section X joined to a thin section Y, and there is a steady current in the wire. How do the currents I_X and I_Y in the two sections compare?

options.text: They are equal: the same charge passes each cross-section per second.
I_Y is greater, since the charges move faster through the narrow section Y.
I_X is greater, since the thick section X holds more of the charge carriers.
It depends on the direction of the current, as current decreases along a wire.

questions.stem: Predict first. A copper wire forms part of a circuit carrying a steady direct current. Which statement about the charge carriers in the wire is correct?

options.text: Free electrons drift slowly towards the positive terminal of the cell.
Electrons travel at close to the speed of light, so a lamp lights at the instant the switch closes.
Protons move along the wire, from the positive terminal towards the negative one.
Electrons leave the cell and some are used up in the lamp, so fewer return to the cell.

questions.explanation: In a metal the charge carriers are free electrons. Being negative, they are attracted towards the positive terminal, and on average they drift only slowly (typically well under 1 mm s⁻¹).
